item.title: America has lost 200k of jobs in media, film and the arts. How much is AI? (480 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.apricitas.io/p/ai-and-the-fall-of-the-creative-class, See on Hacker News

Thanks for reading! If you haven’t subscribed, please click the button below:

By subscribing, you’ll join over 80,000 people who read Apricitas!

America has lost more than 200k jobs in “creative” industries over the last four years, with roughly 50k lost within the last year alone. That makes for one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history, with similar job loss intensity and duration occurring only during the major economic recessions of 2001 and 2008. Yet there’s no generalized recession today—instead, this period of job loss coincides with the rise of AI systems that can compose wholesale novels, photorealistic images, soundalike music, and practically every other form of digital art, en masse and at extremely low costs. Is this the fall of the Creative Class?

Proving the exact amount of AI-driven job loss in the arts is extremely difficult. Media firms are decidedly coy about their AI use, both to protect against public backlash and, more financially important, to preserve the legal basis for their copyrights. The effects of AI are also hard to disentangle from other factors currently affecting arts businesses, like consolidation in Hollywood, offshoring of content production, or the continued displacement of traditional media providers in favor of social media creators. Yet perhaps the clearest evidence of AI’s influence is just that all subsectors of the digital arts industry are losing jobs, while in-person entertainment is still growing at a healthy pace.

Some of those digital job losses are just a continuation of prior trends, like in the publishing industry where technological change has been continually grinding away newspaper and magazine jobs for decades. Yet for sectors like live broadcasting, streaming, or graphic design, recent experience is an unusual downturn compared to the tranquility of years prior. Then there’s the worst-hit sector, movie & sound recording, which has been bleeding jobs at a nearly unprecedented pace over the last three years.

Hollywood has never seen a stretch as bad as the last four years, with the movie & TV industry losing more than 100k jobs, nearly one-third of the sector’s total. At the depths touched this summer, total employment was lower than at any point since the 2008 recession and approaching the lowest point in 30 years. The streaming era has proven an extremely difficult transition, with traditional films and TV shows losing watch time to user-generated and increasingly AI-assisted or AI-generated content flows.

Overall, nearly half the media job losses of the last four years have been concentrated in the movie & sound recording sector that includes Hollywood. Written publishing has been the next-largest source of job loss, with employment down by more than 70k over the same time frame. Yet the job losses have by no means been contained to any particular part of media; instead they’ve hit nearly every subsector at some point. Nor do they show any sign of abating, with losses consistently hovering at around 50k per year and even accelerating in recent months. Will further AI development continue displacing workers in creative industries?

To understand what could happen to the business of art amidst the rise of AI, it’s important to understand what did happen to it during the first digital transition, the rise of the internet.

It was the turn of the millennium, and Metallica had a problem. Demos of their upcoming, unreleased tracks were bouncing around radio and the internet, originally leaked onto a new internet file-sharing website called Napster. There they found thousands of files shared amongst hundreds of thousands of users, many of which were direct rips of albums that sold for $15 being offered for free. The most anticipated albums were often leaked online even before they were on store shelves. Metallica sued Napster for copyright infringement, and they were soon joined by separate suits from other prominent artists and eventually the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA).

Much of the general public was understandably unsympathetic to Metallica, perceived as a bunch of already-successful millionaires trying to bilk even more money from listeners, and were even less sympathetic towards the RIAA, perceived as scurrilous middlemen who take from artists and fans alike. But the two of them easily won their lawsuit, forcing Napster into bankruptcy. Yet Metallica may have been right on the law but were on the wrong side of technology; the RIAA had won the battle but was losing the war.

The modern internet made file-sharing extremely easy, and no matter how much whac-a-mole companies played, they could not possibly catch every illegal upload. The perennial threat of piracy undermined their copyright and limited their ability to charge for music. Eventually, the value of individual songs fell to the point that companies like Spotify and Apple Music could swoop in to acquire massive catalogues, consolidate them, and charge a comparatively trivial fee for access. For what a single Metallica album would have cost in 2000, you can now get a month’s worth of unlimited access to nearly all human-made music.

The music industry has never returned to the heyday paydays of the peak CD era—even without adjusting for inflation, streaming revenue pales in comparison to ‘90s physical media sales. This was a massive boon to consumers, but it was also a squeeze on musicians that forced them to fundamentally change their business model over time. Instead of just selling records to earn money directly, music itself increasingly became a loss-leading advertisement for the live concerts (and merch) that provided a growing share of artists’ income. Tours got longer, venues got bigger, ticket prices skyrocketed, and musicians frequently took on roles closer to public influencers than isolated artistes. Were it not for rising concert sales, the business model of music would have completely collapsed, and the income going to musicians would have cratered.

Of course, there were still significant downsides to the transition into the streaming era. Bands (especially smaller ones) complain about the unending pressure to always be on tour. Musicians whose content was suited to home listening lost out to those more suited to giant festivals. Even accounting for concert revenues, musicians made less money than before. Yet musicians fared better than many areas of entertainment subsectors because there was a live component to fall back on—for many media industries, the digital era left no such comfort.

Over time, the business of video has moved in the opposite direction of music—out of the theatre and into the home. Hollywood formerly made most of its money enticing customers to visit sold-out movie theatres, but these were gradually supplanted by broadcast TV, cable, and physical media. Yet because each successful technological leap increased total video watch time, the industry was still able to thrive amidst technological upheaval. That is, until the modern streaming era.

Today, the plethora of video options and the rise of social media have sent video producers into a vicious competition for limited attention. Even before adjusting for inflation, movie ticket sales ended last year down 25% from their 2019 peak, cable revenue is down 18% from its peak, and streaming revenue has not been able to compensate for the drop. The mountain of free user-generated content on YouTube, Twitch, TikTok, or social media was already presenting harsh competition for traditional video companies in the years before ChatGPT’s launch, and now streaming services are also competing with a flood of AI-generated content. The business model of video media is fundamentally getting squeezed, and unlike in the music industry, there’s basically no equivalent to live concerts that Hollywood can be used to ease the pain.

The actual worst-case scenario for creative workers amidst the AI revolution is something similar to what happened to the publishing industry after the advent of the internet—that is, near-total collapse of their fundamental business model. Newspapers used to employ roughly half a million people in the US, more than the entire oil industry, and now their payrolls are down nearly 85% and still dropping. Magazine publishers likewise have let 66% of their staff go since the 90s, while book publishers have lost 40%.

The routine informational updates that previously formed newspapers’ bread-and-butter were all de-bundled—box scores moved to sports websites, stock movements went to financial websites, forecasts went to weather websites—each loss compounding on itself to undermine consumers’ need to buy the paper. Search engines became the first place people looked to for information, and newspapers’ advertising revenue rapidly started flowing to companies like Google instead. The collective of social media users became faster at breaking any news story than a daily paper could ever hope to be. When papers eventually did start aggressively paywalling content, the internet made it trivially easy for people to just copy the articles’ content and share it beyond the paywall. The entire business model had collapsed, to the point that now only a select few major newspapers can even survive.

That scale of copyright dilution and forced unbundling is the worst-case scenario for media businesses in the age of AI. It’s possible arts jobs could survive via consumers’ deep-seated aversion to explicitly AI-generated content, but AI is increasingly being used throughout media in ways invisible to the average end consumer. Roughly 32% of workers in the overall arts, entertainment, and recreation sector use Generative AI to some extent, which is less than the 62% average across all industries, but still enough that virtually every major media project could have some AI within its workflow.

Indeed, AI is likely seeping into media production processes in ways large companies themselves would struggle to prevent even when they desire to—how can a TV studio be sure nobody in their writers’ room is consulting ChatGPT for jokes or any storyboard artist is generating concept art? And even if professional TV and movie studios do effectively hold out against temptation and prevent internal AI use, how long can they compete with the large mass of wannabe independent creators with much fewer scruples? Plenty of media businesses tried to hold out against the algorithmic content waves of the 2010s and were buried as a result.

Yet fundamentally, it’s difficult to meaningfully predict how new technologies will interact with existing arts businesses. Take the unexpected resurgence in book sales over the last four years. The novel as a commercial art form had been struggling for decades, with fewer books sold in 2019 than at the beginning of the millennium, but the last six years have seen an unprecedented 70% surge in sales. The unlikely savior of the printed word came from perhaps its polar opposite—TikTok.

Of course, fewer people read now than ever before—for the general public, short-form video apps have accelerated the displacement of reading, just as TV, video games, or social media before them. Yet for a dwindling number of dedicated repeat readers, “BookTok” became a new way to source reviews, analysis, discourse, and community in a way that boosted the reading experience and absolutely turbocharged book sales. It’s possible that AI tools could have those same totally unpredictable spillovers for other museums, concerts, or other forms of art in ways that are unpredictable today, in much the same way short-form video saved books in ways that could never have been anticipated beforehand.

At the end of the day, the arts are only a small sector of the overall macroeconomy. Media made up a small share of the labor market even at its peak, and it has always been difficult to get hired in creative industries to the point that making fun of art students’ job prospects became an easy punchline. The movie industry has an income profile closer to eggs or bicycles than something major like healthcare or finance. Were the goal to create art for art’s sake, for the intangible and nonmonetizable cultural benefits, it would be relatively easy to counterbalance any economic impacts of AI on artists just by reversing recent cuts to the National Endowments for the Arts & Humanities.

It’s telling that Anthropic, the most prominent AI lab, has basically never bothered with image, video, or music generation, because the prospective economic benefits are marginal when compared to using AI to tackle math or scientific problems. OpenAI learned this lesson the hard way when it was forced to abandon its video generation platform Sora, deciding it had better use for its limited compute than making synthetic TikToks. Nowadays, the art generation is done primarily by secondary players running smaller models, though even these are large enough to threaten significant disruption to legacy media businesses.

In other words, the primary impacts of AI art will be on culture and society rather than the macroeconomy. Yet arts jobs might be a microcosm for other “creative-adjacent” work that occupies a much larger share of economic activity. Take the tech sector itself, which is the clearest place where AI-driven job loss has shown up outside the media business, as powerful coding agents replace human programmers. Annual tech job gains stood at nearly 300k in 2022, but the sector has been bleeding jobs every year since then in what is now its longest labor market downturn.

Right now, AI-driven job displacement has been relatively minor outside of these few narrow sectors. Unemployment is higher than it was four years ago but still below even the 2010s average, and overall job turnover rates remain extremely low. Some white-collar sectors that looked prime for AI automation have even been on a hiring spree over the last few years, including legal and engineering firms. Yet if the economic impact of AI ends up being anywhere near large enough to validate the trillions of dollars investors are currently betting on it, these economic disruptions will only spread from here.

Discussion about this post

Ready for more?

item.title: We should be more ambitious with the software we build (655 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://danluu.com/ambitious/, See on Hacker News

Since early this year, Michael Malis (of pgrust) has been showing me interesting things he's done and saying

[W]e should be more ambitious1 with the software we build

There is, understandably, a lot of skepticism about projects like pgrust because there are so many low-quality AI-generated projects out there. If I didn't know Malis and didn't look into it, I would just assume that pgrust was another vibe slopped project that's never going to work. But I know Malis well enough to trust his work without looking into it, and if you look into it a bit, you'll see that in testing pgrust, he's testing thoroughly enough that he's even uncovering real bugs in Postgres, such as this numerical bug that can cause valid SP-GiST operations to fail, this format cache bug that can cause incorrect results from JSONPath, this pgcrypto bug that can cause later operations to fail, multiple memory safety bugs in the dictionary loader2, this money overflow bug, etc.

This isn't to say that pgrust is bug free3, but it does indicate that there's a substantial amount of testing happening and, even if pgrust itself is never successful, just making the attempt will have improved Postgres in a durable way. The main pitch for pgrust is actually performance, and that's where the really interesting work is happening; if pgrust fails, it's possible that some of the optimizations they've demonstrated will make it into Postgres, Clickhouse, etc., but that's obviously less direct than filing Postgres bugs which get fixed.

That being said, I find it understandable that, every time I see pgrust discussed on a news aggregator, most people dismiss it as vibeslop garbage because almost all of these rewrite projects are slop. If I didn't know Malis, I would make the same assumption, because who has the time to look into all of these projects? Because I know Malis, I didn't bother to look at it; I just trusted him (I only found the above because I wanted to check on pgrust before using it as an example for this post).

As a consumer of software, everywhere you look, there's slow software that the creator is claiming is fast because the creator is touting some slop benchmark, e.g., here's one of multiple examples I saw yesterday, and of course low-quality software that doesn't work is more common than ever.

But, as a builder of software, it doesn't matter that almost all of these projects are vibeslop, that other people are out there shoveling out huge piles of crap and calling it gold. You can build things like pgrust or other projects that would've been too large to really be feasible in the past and, if you do a reasonable job with testing and benchmarking, that stuff can actually be good-enough quality to use.

If I were writing it, I would say "we can be more ambitious with the software we build" and not "we should", but Malis has been casually chatting with me when he's said this, so maybe he would say the same in an actual post; don't read too much into should vs. can here. What's interesting to me is how capabilities have advanced such that we can do a lot more.

Just for example, after hearing that OpenAI was going to use Cerebras for their SOTA models and not just fast-but-low-quality models like 5.3-Codex-Spark, I looked at where time on my computer would go if I was using a SOTA model, but 10x to 100x faster; some things that were already sometimes a bottleneck that would only get worse with a faster model were:

  1. Ripgrep
  2. Compiling Rust
  3. Syscall and filesystem overhead

At the level of a "works for me" project, these are all things that can seriously be improved. I don't have much spare time at the moment but, even so, I built this regex engine that can be tweaked to be faster than other general-purpose regex libraries on any particular workload I care about, this ripgrep fork that uses the native code compiler from the regex engine and is faster for my codex ripgrep workloads (of course a text index is the better solution, but I've already worked on text indexing and this was a "just for fun" project where I wasn't trying to do the optimal thing), and a Rust that sped up builds for my projects (huge improvement for cold builds, moderate for warm, limited by wanting to avoid forking the Rust compiler front-end). For syscalls and filesystem overhead, just switching development from Mac to Linux improved this a lot, and of course this is another thing that can be sped up a lot as well, especially when agents are hammering lots of small filesystem operations (it's not uncommon to see my machine waiting on filesystem ops because the standard OS filesystem interface wasn't designed with modern disk performance in mind).

For someone like me who doesn't know anything about regexes, string matching algorithms, compilers, interpreters, etc., this set of projects would've taken a year or more to get to "works for me" quality. Instead, this was a low single-digit number of hours of my time. If I wanted to make any of these things meet a "useful product or open source project" quality bar, that would be a lot more work0, but it's still pretty incredible how much this process is sped up.

Another project I previously mentioned was this Azul AI which is superhuman at matched time controls. When I did that (with GPT-5.1/5.2), with zero AI knowledge, it took about 5 hours of my time to get something superhuman, and about 20 hours of my time to become what appeared to be the strongest AI at the time, including being stronger against humans than this AI that was used to cheat on Board Game Arena. Gabriel Cangussu recently built an AI that demolishes my AI, and AFAICT, it took him substantially less time than my AI took me. From talking to him about it, one key difference is that Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 have a much better understanding of board game AIs. When I used GPT-5.1/5.2, pretty much every suggestion they had was wrong and I had to do a lot of steering to get things to be remotely reasonable. If I had GPT read a codebase or a paper to implement relevant techniques from the paper, it would fail. If I read the paper myself and named a technique, it would say it did the technique, but it would generally do something that superficially looked like the technique but wasn't the actual technique until I issued some corrections. When the model is that far from being able to do the right thing, if you have no background in the area, it's fairly time consuming to check if the model did the right thing since you have to learn enough about what it's supposed to do to be able to check that it did what was claimed.

When I did that project, I said to friends that I didn't think the state models were in could last. It seemed impossible that they wouldn't get good enough to be able to read a paper and implement the techniques soon, and it seemed like they should also be able to pick out codebases and papers to crib from as well. From my experience messing around a bit with Fable 5 and Cangussu's experience with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, that seems to have happened, which is a huge time saver for someone like me who doesn't know anything about board game AIs (I know a little bit now, but still less than any real AI researcher)4.

For any particular domain, like board game AIs, you can say, "who cares? Board game AIs don't matter", but I've found this increase in capability to be true in quite a few different domains. Just for example, I did this toy eval of verification and test techniques with GPT-5.6 Sol implementing zstd on medium and xhigh. I haven't had time to write it up, but when I published that post, I also re-did the evals with GPT-6 Astra. 6 Astra was so good that I had to find different evals because models had advanced too much. For zstd, 6 Astra succeeds at passing all of the registered tests more than 99% of the time across all conditions, even the ones that significantly impair performance, like using TDD (and, BTW, it does it more cheaply as well, taking about $1 to implement zstd). I ended up using the IMAP RFC, which 5.6 Sol couldn't do effectively, and Pandoc, which is a pretty major thing to implement as it needs to be able to read and write many different formats5.

BTW, when people have said they used the new model and everything just works, software is solved, etc., I haven't found this to be true at all. It's true that there are a lot more things the newer model can one-shot, where things basically just work, but this just means that I end up working on more ambitious things where models still struggle6. I'm more productive and can work faster, but I find that, in terms of what I'm doing, I get farther from "it just works" with each more capable model because the gap between what the model can verify effectively without significant handholding and what the model can implement has been increasing7. All of that is a long-winded and less eloquent way of saying: we should be more ambitious with the software we build.

Thanks to Laurence Tratt, Yossi Kreining, Alex Kolovsky, and Michael Malis for comments/corrections/discussion.

I've had this note on my recent posts, which also applies to this one. In order to get more posts out, I'm trying to crank posts out in half an hour and not review them much. This definitely means less well-supported posts. If I were writing this in my standard style, I would've had comprehensive benchmarks for all of my projects that I mentioned. Instead, I did a quick comparison that satisfied my curiosity and am writing this up without rigorous benchmarking, and there are maybe twenty or thirty things in this post that I'd like to do but haven't done.

Appendix: we should be less ambitious with the software we build

Here's a comment from Yossi Kreinin, quoted (with permission, of course):

If you publish this I will publish a response explaining that for most people they should be less ambitious with the software they build with AI or they'll experience abject failure. I think a lot of the problems don't lend themselves that well to "agentic loops" since you don't have clear pass/fail criteria, and even when you do most people have trouble reasoning about giant black boxes which they can impose constraints on but can't understand the innards of [I include myself in this set.] This is a little bit like microservices I guess, where some people both need it and are very good at using it but likely for most people, they need it less and can't use it well at all. I sort of envy the ones who should and actually can be this ambitious about the software they build of course; not saying you shouldn't be more ambitious at all but moderating said ambition is a big part of handling the current situation for most I think

I have a similar thought about "there's no reason for software to be slow" BTW; in many cases, if you use AI to speed up some flow, you will add a bunch of messy code that will be overfit for the use case you tested on and will neither generalize, perf-wise, for all the use cases you should care about, nor will be maintainable upon future changes. If you know what you're doing and you understand how the system should be decomposed into parts and when it makes sense to go all-in on optimizing some part or a combination of them working together and how to properly benchmark it, etc., then things are great, but if for instance you have a manager who thinks there's no reason for software to be slow and he pushes people to use AI to make random parts of the software fast... Run for cover

My feeling is that, overall, the situation here is a bit analogous to the discussion here about why I don't like when people talk about how AI gives a 100x or 1000x productivity increase. There are some things that are sped up by a very large factor, easily over 1000000x. And some things don't currently get sped up at all. If you do exactly what you would've done five years ago, but with AI, the speedup is fairly poor because of Amdahl's law. But, in the general case, you can choose what to speed up and if you're looking for things that are productive to do, this often seems to involve things that were previously too expensive to do.

And, I think that you can often set up systems that have some kind of self-checking property even when most people wouldn't. This discussion of the implementation of Guards of Atlantis 2 is an example of that. It's a poor choice for an AI project because the official rules are a mess of ambiguous and contradictory English text (it's probably the game I've seen humans misplay at the highest rate, and the rules are confusing enough that the designer has often changed their mind about what their own rules mean despite continually maintaining that the rules are perfectly clear and one can play the game by simply reading the rules as written). If you try to produce a working set of rules in a naive way, AI won't really help with this (although it can speed up implementation once you have a clean spec), but for that, I was able to set up some kind of janky set of consistency checks between all of the inconsistent explanations of the game rules, which got fairly close to a correct set of rules (approximately as close as what someone else did with much more human effort and less of a systematic approach), which was enough to compare it to someone else's implementation and get a working set of rules. This setup did cost a lot more in tokens than a more manual approach. But it was "only" a month or two of the $200/mo OpenAI subscription with GPT-5.1/5.2, which is a lower cost than the cost in time of me sitting down and writing a clean spec for the game, i.e., a copy of the rules that is actually consistent and correct.

I feel like a lot of problems are in something like this class of problem, where it's possible to set up some kind of at least partially self-checking setup that a human can spend a small amount of time on. This also feels analogous to the situation about software testing at large, where (before coding agents) I found fuzzing and property-based testing to be highly effective. For most domains, people told me some kind of reason this kind of testing wouldn't work, but when I've tried these techniques with all of the domains people told me these techniques don't work for, they work fine. They're somewhat more work to apply, but they're still applicable and, AFAICT, more efficient and effective than writing traditional unit tests.

Part of the gist of Yossi's comment is that people aren't doing this kind of thing. Considering how many more bugs I see now than I used to, e.g., the last time I opened up the web chat for a big AI lab, I ran into a double-digit number of bugs within one minute, it's hard to say that Yossi is wrong. But, to that point, I still have my original opinion. Just because other people are pumping out vast quantities of barely working slop doesn't mean that you have to do the same thing.

Appendix: a few "random" examples

The examples in the body of the post I gave for things I've done are tooling things I never would've done. There are a lot more things like that as well since it's so easy to build "works for me" quality tooling that's intended solely for me. I do think it's possible to go further than is productive, e.g., Steve Yegge wrote a lot about Gas Town and how productive it was, but when he was building his next agentic framework, he noted that he never used Gas Town to successfully build anything other than Gas Town, people were into Ralph Loops for a while even though, when I tried comparing them, they seemed worse than just doing the naive thing I was doing at the time, normal loops with context where you sometimes clear context as appropriate instead of doing it by default at the completely arbitrary point of when a single turn is completed, etc., so I've tried to stick to things where the impact is pretty direct. Besides the obvious reason this has been effective, the dramatic change in model and harness capability over time means that what tooling it makes sense to build changes very quickly, so spending a lot of time working on any particular tool that will be suboptimal at best and quite possibly obsolete in three months doesn't really make sense.

And, for a lot of my personal tools, my assumption is that an AI lab will obsolete anything I make in short order. For a very silly example of this, I have a tool that was useful since the release of GPT-5.6 Sol that restarts codex when it finds a memory leak. Presumably, OpenAI will fix this at some point and this tool will become worthless. For a slightly less silly example, take the Rust interpreter I had some agent build. For token-budget reasons, a lot of things that ought to be done for a very high-performance interpreter haven't been done.

For example, the interpreter doesn't modify the actual Rust front-end compiler to make it easy to take updates; performance would be much better if I just made changes to the Rust front-end, but I don't have the token budget to maintain a compatible fork of the Rust compiler, but this shouldn't be a problem for OpenAI. OpenAI spent $10B+ on getting access to Cerebras while also preventing Anthropic from having access.

Funnily enough, for coding, on many tasks, if you actually use one of their SOTA models and compare it to what you get from Anthropic, the actual speedup isn't all that large because of time spent on things like compiling Rust. Given that they were willing to commit $10B+ on this, it stands to reason that they'll eventually do a better job at speeding up the relevant tools than anyone could feasibly do outside an AI lab, so there's not much point in spending too much effort on this (this could arguably be untrue if non-coding tasks are expected to completely dominate future OpenAI revenue in the short term, but even then, given what they pay for tokens vs. what I pay, it still seems like it would make sense for them to speed a lot of these things up given that I could do it outside of a lab; perhaps there's some kind of argument like, if you have access to their usage data, there are so many more important bottlenecks that this one doesn't make sense to prioritize, but it still seems like it should make sense for them at some point even if it doesn't fall into the top 100 bottlenecks for Cerebras-enabled coding agents).

Another kind of thing that one might not call ambitious, but that speaks to the kind of thing that's possible, are games that I've made. There are games I've thought about and wanted to make that I don't think are generally enjoyable enough that they make sense for a real audience, but that I've wanted to play. For example, ever since reading David Gerrold's Star Wolf books in the 90s, I've wanted to play a game that implements combat as described in the books, which is a sort of like submarine combat. At least among realistic war games, this genre is extremely niche because almost everybody finds naval combat boring, and submarine combat is a particularly boring subgenre of naval combat games, so this doesn't really make sense as a money-making game, but it's so easy to implement games that I had an agent implement the game so I could play it for an hour or two. I never would've spent 10-20 hours implementing a game so that I could play it for an hour or two, but I'd spend 5 minutes. I've also previously mentioned implementing a game with the same rules as Scout and Guards of Atlantis 2. I was never going to take the time to implement these games by hand just so I have a way to play with my friends on the occasions where we can't get together in-person, but I'm happy to have an LLM bash these things out. And, of course, for people who want to make games with a wider audience, there's a game renaissance going on right now due to coding agents. It's pretty amazing how many interesting and creative games are being made now that having programming skills and the time to put them to use is no longer a bottleneck for making games.

Data analysis is another thing where the productivity multiplier can be very high and I can do all sorts of things I never would've done. As I've mentioned in a number of my last posts, I have way too many of these projects to really be able to write them up, even when attempting to write very quickly and bash out posts in half an hour apiece.

When I've talked to people about their one-off tooling, there's a lot of fun stuff people have done. For example, here's something Peter Geoghegan mentioned a month or two back:

I had Fable implement a custom Neovim Lua function that formats code according to my very specific preferences. This is both something I don't want to maintain myself and inherently a Rube Goldberg device. Theoretically I could accomplish the same outcome in a principled way by patching clang-format, but my requirements are so exact that I think that approach would never be satisfactory.

We use a tool call pgindent, which is our fork of bsd_indent. You can approximate the same formatting rules using clang-format, but that isn't good enough. If I commit something that isn't perfectly formatted/indented according to pgindent, I get a CI failure that I'm expected to fix quickly -- something I'd really prefer to avoid ...

Practically speaking, getting slick, clang-format-style formatting that avoids nag emails about misindented code requires a total architectural mess (I also don't want to spend the time developing a principled approach, but that's really a separate issue). The function allows me to effortlessly format a given block of code from Neovim, similar to the clang-format LSP integration. I'm being unreasonably fussy here, of course, but I find that LLMs allow me to be this exacting about tooling.

The function performs multiple passes: an initial formatting pass using clang-format/clangd, and a separate formatting pass using pgindent. I need it to do both because clang-format handles some cases correctly that pgindent misses. This is brittle because I only want to format the code within a range of lines selected via block visual mode (I don't want to run clang-format on code not added by my patch). This conflicts with pgindent's design; it can only format whole C files.

Figuring out which relevant subset of the temp whole file buffer needs to be copied back into my working buffer is nontrivial. The initial line range I selected doesn't directly map to the affected C AST elements. So the function uses tree-sitter to intelligently delineate the exact subset of the temp indented C code that needs to be copied back. The rules need to be fuzzy in exactly the right way for cases where my selection straddles the same block of code. There are a bunch of edge cases.

Another complicating factor is that pgindent relies on a typedef file generated with objdump to identify types; without that file, the formatting looks wonky. The formatting function dynamically generates any extra typedefs from clangd, for that one file, so I don't have to worry about a stale typedef file (I might have created a new struct seconds before running the formatting tool, I don't want to run objdump on the whole postgres binary each time, that'd blow up latency).

This appears to work perfectly. The latency is totally acceptable. I have only a vague understanding of how all this works, though. I don't even know Lua. This will probably continue to work, even as further changes are made to our fork of bsd_indent that somewhat alter how code is formatted, which happens from time to time.

I'm skeptical of the saaspocalypse. But I do think that LLMs are writing a lot of useful software that would have been insanely uneconomical to write any other way. There's an interesting small subset of software that'd be impossibly tedious for any human to maintain, relative to the value that it creates.

I also caught with Malis while writing this and found out about all sorts of fun stuff he's been doing. It's enough that writing it all up in detail could be its own post, but one fun thing is that, the last time I taked to him about pgrust verification, he mentioned using Kani to verify some parts of the code. He's since switched to Lean and has been using Lean to verify things that are too complex to do in Kani. This would be another topic for another post, but I wonder why people have generally settled on Lean for LLM-driven proofs (as opposed to, say, ACL2). I wonder how Lean would look in an updated version of this theorem prover comparison, or if someone were to run a theorem prover eval that's analogous to this language eval.

Of course, you can think of plenty of examples out of AI labs, such as a mid-sized team Anthropic building an internal replacement for GitHub as well as some other tooling in five months

A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months.

I think these kinds of examples are interesting and they point to where the industry will be in the not-so-far future, but what you can do with unlimited tokens, while relying on other infrastructure and tooling built with unlimited tokens doesn't tell you much about what you can accomplish today without unlimited funds. Projects like pgrust as well as projects that people I know do in their spare time (of which I've probably mentioned something like 1%—there are just a lot of these, like David Turner creating an skipper for podcasts that's "works for me" quality that works better than anything he could find, the spare-time projects Dennis Snell mentioned here, etc.) are more representative of what you can do today.

item.title: Small Programs and Languages (169 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ratfactor.com/cards/pl-small, See on Hacker News

Page started: 2025-06-02

Page published: 2026-07-28

My Implementing a Forth article got some great feedback, particularly around the subject of tiny Forth implementations. (And it was an excuse to list some of the tiniest Forths I’ve seen.)

I know I’m not alone in seeing the appeal of tiny Forths, tiny languages, tiny programs, and just small stuff in general. What’s up with that, anyway?

The appeal of tiny programs

Tiny programs are approachable.

If I see that something is 200 lines of code, I’m much more likely to read it than if it’s 2,000 or 20,000 lines.

What’s more, if it’s a program that does something interesting in 20 lines when I was expecting 2,000, then I’m going to be very, very interested to read those 20 lines!

When I was researching DOM diffing libraries prior to creating RetroV, one of the repos I looked at was ijk by Luke Jackson.

I was pretty used to looking at fat JavaScript libraries at that point, so when I cracked open the source file for ijk, I was really surprised. Here’s the source: index.js (githubusercontent.com).

Just 25 lines! I was instantly intrigued.

More recently, one of the responses to my aforementioned Forth article was Philippe Brochard with a 46 byte "Forth".

46 bytes!

It’s so small, I can just put the hexdump right here:

50b8 8e00 31d8 e8ff 0017 003c 0575 00ea
5000 3c00 7401 eb02 e8ee 0005 0588 eb47
b8e6 0200 d231 14cd e480 7580 c3f4

Sure, very few people jump at a chance to read raw machine code. But that’s exactly my point. Something this small doesn’t feel so scary, right? I mean, 46 bytes. If you put the effort into it, you know you can figure out how it works eventually.

This next one almost serves as a counter-example because the code is so dense and frightening, but I can’t help mentioning it anyway.

One of my favorite software stories is Roger K.W. Hui’s Appendix A "Incunabulum" from An Implementation of J in which he describes Arthur Whitney writing an array-based language interpreter,

"…​on one page and in one afternoon — an interpreter fragment on the AT&T 3B1 computer. I studied this interpreter for about a week for its organization and programming style…​"

Hui can list the entire interpreter in the appendix because it’s just that single page, 122 lines of incredibly cryptic C, which you can view here:

I haven’t personally tackled that puzzle yet, but it’s in my unwritten list of dense computer things that I would print out and take with me if I suddenly found myself cast out of society and forced to go live alone up on a mountain or something.

(By the way, J is in the family of array languages which include APL. If you enjoy brevity, cryptic programming puzzles, and high performance numerical computing, these languages have got you covered!)

Update July 2026: Speaking of Arthur Whitney, Alex (alexalejandre.com) sent me a link that I knew I’d have to add here. Check this out: https://fall.tr/kos

It’s a transcript of a Geo Carncross talk describing an operating system, kOS, featuring Whitney’s k array language, kdb database, and a GUI and window manager in a 90 Kb bootable image. Individual source code stats are just as impressive (such as 60 lines of C for the aforementioned GUI and window manager). And apparently kdb is 100 lines of C? Is that right? Even Whitney C, that’s still impressive. Now I’m even more intrigued by kdb than ever! And if any of that seems interesting, you’ll definitely enjoy the article Impending kOS (vector.org.uk).

Something else that would certainly need to be in the collection I take to that lonely mountain would have to be The Most Beautiful Program Ever Written, according to the title of a talk by William Byrd. Spoiler alert: It’s this Lisp interpreter in Lisp:

(define eval-expr
  (lambda (expr env)
    (pmatch expr
      [`,x (guard (symbol? x))
        (env x)]
      [`(lambda (,x) ,body)
        (lambda (arg)
          (eval-expr body (lambda (y)
                            (if (eq? x y)
                                arg
                                (env y)))))]
      [`(,rator ,rand)
       ((eval-expr rator env)
        (eval-expr rand env))])))

Recreation or fundamental truths?

Now, we all know that code golfing (wikipedia.org) is a programmer’s recreational game, and just for fun, right?

But is any of this actually useful?

I say yes. And I’ll go one step further: They are meaningful.

When you see a ray tracer that fits on a business card (fabiensanglard.net), it makes you realize that a ray tracer is something that can fit on a business card!

That’s an actual fact about the minimum complexity of ray tracers.

"…​the length of a shortest computer program (in a predetermined programming language) that produces the object as output."

(I learned about Kolmogorov complexity in a book about Kurt Gödel and it was my favorite thing in what was otherwise a pretty dry and depressing book.)

The meaning I get from this is that code golfers, for the benefit of the whole human race, produce versions of programs that represent the minimum complexity of those programs. Way to go code golfers!

What do we know about the fundamental complexity of the Lisp programming language?

That’s a fact about Lisps with garbage collection. When you strip everything else away, you can get the essentials down to 436 bytes!

I take comfort in this because that means the concept can be boiled down to this hand-held size. And that means I can probably fit it in my head.

Thanks to Frank Force, we know that a 3D browser game can fit in 2Kb of (insanely compressed) JavaScript source: A 3D game in 2Kb of JS (frankforce.com)

And we haven’t even scraped the surface of what the demoscene has to offer for computers going back to the 1980s. Here’s a good place to start: https://demoscene.assembly.org/

Mini-things are fun and useful and meaningful.

My point here is that you don’t have to actually study the intricate clockwork puzzle of a miniaturized/golfed program to benefit from it. The miniature simply serves to prove that the concept can fit on a business card and it can fit in your head. Go ahead and find a readable version to study instead. (The miniature will likely have many things to teach, but some of them will be about how to make miniature programs.)

Small languages

Small programs are interesting. But I’m also interested in small programming languages.

Generally speaking, the smaller the language, the less expressive it is.

One of the most well-known, least expressive languages is assembly.

Assembly languages are very syntactically and conceptually simple. There’s not much language at all: it’s mostly a rigid sequence of opcode mnemonics. Even with macros, writing in assembly is mostly about understanding the puzzle of a particular CPU’s instruction set architecture, or ISA. (You can prove this by comparing the syntax of assembly for CISC and RISC processors. The puzzle is totally different, while the language remains practically unchanged.)

An honorable mention must be made here for SNOBOL, which is kind of like assembly language both for the rigid syntactic reasons listed above and also because it presents a similar control flow challenge. Like a CPU, it only understands jumps and call/return. (In every other way, SNOBOL is wildly different, being a string matching and replacing language. It’s weird and fun and highly effective.)

Moving on to syntactically tiny "high-level" languages, these three are brilliant:

  • Forths win just about any "smallness" contest. The only syntactical construct is the space character. Forths are mind-bendingly flexible and powerful in a way that is downright disturbing.

  • Lisps, (especially Scheme?), have small core languages with very simple syntax and enormous expressive power and flexibility.

  • Tcl deserves to be mentioned with Forth and Lisp. Tcl is wild because everything is a string in a way that is hard to appreciate at first. You can construct your own language in Tcl just as you can with Forth or Lisp.

Forth, Lisp, and Tcl only require you to understand a few core ideas and give you limitless power in return. You could fit the syntactic core of these languages on an index card or less.

And yet, to wield these tools effectively requires a massive shift in thinking if you’re used to "normal" Algol-like procedural languages.

So how about something that is both small and simple and doesn’t require a blood sacrifice?

I think the Lua programming language fits the bill. Check out how small the core language is:

I’ve got the printed book version of this document and it’s a thin book! The Lua language is covered in the beginning and it is just 27 pages. 27 pages! I have game manuals longer than that.

The C language is pretty small. I don’t think it’s super easy to program effectively and safely with C, but there’s no denying it’s compact and pretty expressive for its size.

Newcomer Zig is C-like. But I think it’s actually quite large and you need to know a lot of it to use it effectively. (I’m also a fan of Zig and think it’s totally worth it. The size is there for a reason.)

JavaScript has a core language that is quite small. Probably on par with Lua, actually. Functions, arrays, and objects (used as dictionaries) are pretty much all the JS I use and I like it that way!

As with the natural human languages, the trade-off with a bigger programming language is, hopefully, greater expressivity.

Small or expressive. Which way should you lean?

In a wonderful talk by David Ungar (wikipedia.org) titled Self and Self: Whys and Wherefores, he laments the mistake of Self’s multiple inheritance:

"It’s far better to make a system a little too simple so a person has to write extra stuff, even write it twice with a comment that says, 'Look over here,' than to have a system that acts in strange ways and nobody can understand why. So, simplicity trumps expressiveness."

Got that? Here’s the bullet from the slide to help you remember:

I think small languages can also be fairly expressive, but only with very, very careful design. Recall Forth, Lisp, and Tcl.

Microworlds: The idea of small, self-contained, learnable programming environments also has a David Ungar connection I discovered while watching his talk. See "ARK" on my Microworlds card. (Smith and Ungar co-created the Self language (selflanguage.org), which is a notable milestone in programming and still under active development to this day.)

Languages which come with full-featured interactive IDEs are obvious potential microworlds.

But I also think that traditional text file-based programming can give you the microworld experience as well. For that, a language needs high quality documentation that installs alongside the compiler/interpreter. And it should strive to have error output that can be understood by beginners, including explanations of what went wrong and hints for how to fix it or or where to find more information.

Libraries: Another easily overlooked aspect of a programming language’s apparent size is its "standard library" of functions, data structures, and methods.

I think function libraries are subject to the exact same size versus expressiveness challenge.

For example, learning the Ramda (ramdajs.com) functional programming library for JavaScript was very much like learning a new programming language and I never managed to learn all of it. The composability of Ramda and the consistency of its curried functions was extremely eye-opening to me. My advice: A little bit of Ramda goes a long way!

The feels: Concision in our tools has a certain quality that goes beyond utility. Little things just spark joy, you know?

Why are small things so delightful?

The appeal of tiny things in general

I’ve always had a fascination with miniatures, dioramas, and tiny scale models.

I know I’m not alone!

Stephanie M. Langin-Hooper, author of Figurines in Hellenistic Babylonia writes in Tiny Things and Why We Love Them (cambridgeblog.org):

"…​the act of shrinking a life-size thing to a smaller scale has an influential effect. The object is now cute, more accessible, more delicate, more 'squee'. It is also more helpless, and thus controllable – comforting and completely non-threatening due to its diminutive size.

Which is exactly the reaction I have when I see a tiny bit of code that does something useful.

Also, I’m super okay with "controllable" in the context of a computer, but the feeling of that paragraph changes a bit if we’re talking about, say, dolls.

Small scale helps make "big" things approachable:

"What might be threatening to think about in the real-scale world can be more manageable and more conceivable in miniature."

Small things, "allow low-stakes experimentation," which is why we often build tiny models of things before we scale them up.

Simon Garfield, author of In Miniature: How Small Things Illuminate the World has many of the same answers. He writes in Small world: Why we love tiny things (theguardian.com):

"The answer lies in our desire for mastery and elucidation. The ability to enhance a life by bringing scaled-down order and illumination to an otherwise chaotic world – a world over which we may otherwise feel we have little control – cannot be overvalued. […​] At its simplest, the miniature shows us how to see, learn and appreciate more with less."

I think this is a big part of what I get out of Assembly Nights with the small scale and orderly logic and internal consistency. Unlike the vast, fathomless Real World, an offline computer is a fantasy place where I can believe I could understand everything if I just tried hard enough for long enough.

"The satisfaction of observing small things becomes a desire to make small things, and both stages address the human need for comprehension and order. We live in a huge and doomy universe, and controlling just a tiny scaled-down part of it restores our sense of order and worth."

I’ve been studying computer history for a little while and I’ve only scratched the surface. But one of the things I’ve been finding is that a lot of the "big" stuff in our field are just accumulations of lots of "little" victories as individuals have solved "little" problems in new and different ways.

"We create small universes in which we may bury ourselves to the exclusion of all else. Blocking out real life for a while – always the prerequisite of the dedicated domestic hobby, from doll’s house modeller to jigsaw enthusiast to adult book colourist – may be contemplative, meditative, blinkered and essential. The people crouching over tiny details as if the world depended on it are only doing it because their world does depend on it."
